faq.q: What is the best angle to film yourself dancing?
faq.a: Straight on from the front, with the phone at about hip to chest height, is the best main angle because it's how an audience sees you. Add a side angle now and then to check posture and the real height of your legs, and film from behind when you're learning from a video so left and right match.

faq.q: How far away should the camera be when filming dance?
faq.a: Usually 3 to 5 metres for one dancer, and 4 to 6 metres for a couple. The test is simple: on your mark, with your arms up and on your biggest travelling step, you should stay in frame with space above your hands and below your feet. If the room is too small, use the 0.5× wide lens and stay near the centre of the frame.

faq.q: Should I film dance videos in portrait or landscape?
faq.a: Landscape for practice, because it leaves room to travel and keeps your feet in frame. Portrait is fine for videos made for social media, or K-pop covers filmed front-on like a fancam, as long as your whole body fits.

faq.q: How do I film myself dancing without a tripod?
faq.a: Prop the phone on a bookshelf against a stack of books, or on a chair placed on a table, so it sits at about hip to chest height. Lean it back slightly, check the framing with a short test, and mark the spot with tape so you can set up the same way next time.

faq.q: What frame rate should I use to record dance practice?
faq.a: 30 fps is fine for most practice. Use 60 fps for turns, jumps and fast footwork so slowed-down replays stay smooth. Save 120 or 240 fps slow motion for checking a single jump or turn, in good light.

faq.q: Does watching videos of yourself really improve your dancing?
faq.a: It helps you see what you can't feel. In a small study of three competitive dancers, scoring their own videos against a checklist improved every move that was tracked. Video works best alongside a teacher's feedback, not instead of it.
